# Design: ai-model-routing

Status: v1.655, 2026-11-25 (v1.655, tests: each paragraph of README `## Running it in production` is placed by the paragraph next to it, not by a count from the section's end, and the v1.652 and v1.653 size tests take out one list of the paragraphs added after v1.653, with README.md and every transcript keeping their bytes (row T30); v1.654, docs and tests: README `## Running it in production` ends with one sentence on `report --opportunities`, whose savings are hypothetical and no return on a training, hosting or build cost, so the section is 24,690 bytes, with every transcript keeping its bytes (row OPP1c); v1.653, docs and tests: README `## Running it in production` gets back the caveats that a trial's time runs from your call to the route's answer and that a self-hosted row's throughputs and hour split are an approximation, eight clauses stated in 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.7, 7, 8.2 or 11 traded out, so the section is 23,976 bytes, with every transcript keeping its bytes (row PROD1h); v1.652, docs and tests: README `## Running it in production`'s nine paragraphs that earlier parts trimmed keep their lead claims, names, quotes and links in 14,010 bytes instead of 15,176, each dropped clause stated in 4.1, 4.3, 4.6, 4.7, 5.2, 7, 8.1, 8.3 or 11, so the section is 23,992 bytes, with every transcript keeping its bytes (row PROD1gbbbbb); v1.651, docs and tests: README `## Running it in production`'s paragraphs on task scopes, a tenant's policy and pinned calls keep their lead claims, names, quotes and links in 3,872 bytes instead of 4,271, each dropped clause stated in 5.2 or 7, with every transcript keeping its bytes (row PROD1gbbbb); earlier versions are in CHANGELOG.md)

## 1. Problem
- A product or pipeline makes the same kind of model call many times: triage a support ticket, extract invoice fields, write a unit test, grade an answer against a rubric. Each such kind of call is a **task**: a repeated call with an **acceptance check** that says whether one output is right (agreement with a gold label, exact match on extracted fields, generated tests passing, a rubric pass)
- Sending every call of a task to the strongest model wastes money; sending it to the cheapest model silently lowers quality, and nothing in the logs says so
- The fix is to route per task: measure each candidate model's **success rate** against the task's acceptance check on a calibration set, and pick the cheapest model whose measured rate clears the task's bar with statistical confidence, with fallback when a call fails, a log of every attempt, and cost rolled up by any tag
- Judge and eval calls are the first-class use case, because a wrong judge corrupts every decision downstream of it and because a judge must not grade its own family's output (generator isolation, 5.2). Nothing in the routing rules is specific to judging: the library has no notion of a domain beyond a task name, its bar and its acceptance counts

## 2. Two flavors, one algorithm
- `cost_effective`: among models that clear the bar, pick the one with the lowest expected cost per call; ties go to higher quality
- `cost_blind`: identical pipeline, but the router treats token cost as 0, so among models that clear the bar it picks the highest quality. Fallback, monitoring and attribution are unchanged; the log still records list-price cost so spend stays visible
- The flavor changes exactly one thing: the `routing_cost` used to rank candidates

## 3. Package layout (Python 3.10+, standard library only)
```
model_routing/
  __init__.py     re-exports every public name below
  __main__.py     `python -m model_routing` runs `cli.main`
  registry.py     Model, Registry
  tasks.py        Task, Cascade (v1.535), load_tasks
  stats.py        wilson_lower_bound, items_needed (v1.140), Stats, calibrate_from_results, item_outcomes (v1.602, 4.3)
  priors.py       Priors
  procedures.py   Procedure, ProcedureResult, ProcedureRun, ProcedureLimitError (v1.576, 4.5)
  budget.py       Budget, BudgetLedger, BudgetExceeded, load_budgets (v1.595, 4.6), billing_bound (v1.597)
  promotion.py    paired_promotion, PromotionCheck (v1.601, 4.7), pair_outcomes (v1.603, 4.7)
  router.py       Candidate, RouteDecision, Router, NoModelClearsBar, reason codes
  providers.py    Completion, ProviderError, Provider, FakeProvider, OpenAICompatibleProvider
  executor.py     Attempt, CallResult, Executor, AllModelsFailed
  monitor.py      Monitor, load_records, load_audits, report, budget_report (v1.598), shadow_pairs (v1.610), pair_results (v1.613), audited_results (v1.632), drift_check (v1.633)
  evaluate.py     Outcome, outcomes_from_rows, load_outcomes, split_items, evaluate (v1.3, section 12)
  delegation.py   DelegationDecision, mode and reason constants, the logic of Router.decide_delegation (v1.4, section 13)
  delegation_eval.py  evaluate_delegation, offline evidence for the inline-or-sub-agent decision (v1.19, section 13.9)
  demo.py         run_demo
  cli.py          main
  py.typed        empty PEP 561 marker: type checkers read the package's own annotations (v1.114)
  data/
    models.json         public list prices and context windows (section 9)
    priors.json         leaderboard-derived priors (section 9)
    example_tasks.json  judge and non-judge example tasks used by the CLI defaults and docs
tests/            owned by the QA author; the implementer never edits it
```
- `json_validator` (section 7) lives in `executor.py`
- v1.507: `estimate_prompt_tokens` (section 7, row FIT1) lives in `executor.py` too
- `model_routing.DATA_DIR` is the `pathlib.Path` of the packaged `data/` folder
- v1.114, packaging: `model_routing/py.typed` is an empty file, the PEP 561 marker that tells a type checker in a user's project to read the annotations of the package instead of treating it as untyped, and `pyproject.toml` ships it as package data beside the data files, `[tool.setuptools.package-data]` `model_routing = ["data/*.json", "py.typed"]`, so a built wheel carries it. The version has one source, `__version__` in `model_routing/__init__.py`: `pyproject.toml` writes no `version` under `[project]`, lists `"version"` in its `dynamic` list and reads it with `[tool.setuptools.dynamic]` `version = { attr = "model_routing.__version__" }`. `__version__` stays one top-level assignment of a string literal of the form `X.Y.Z`, and the only binding of that name in the file, so the build backend reads it from the source without importing the package. Chosen over a test that two written copies agree, because a value written once cannot drift. The version stays 0.1.0 here. Checked by `tests/test_packaging.py`: the marker exists and is empty, the package data is exactly those two entries, the version is dynamic and read from that attribute, the literal is the one binding, and where the distribution `ai-model-routing` is installed in the running interpreter (an editable install, as CI makes), its metadata version equals `model_routing.__version__`; with no such install that last test skips. The two tests that read `pyproject.toml` (the package data and the dynamic version) load a TOML parser inside the test with `pytest.importorskip`, `tomllib` from Python 3.11 and `tomli` before it (pytest itself depends on `tomli` there), so where that parser does not load only those two skip and the other four still run, the marker among them (v1.121). `tests/test_packaging_skips.py` runs `tests/test_packaging.py` in a child pytest of the same interpreter twice, as is and with that parser's name set to `None` in `sys.modules` before collection, and checks that both runs hold the same six tests, that the block turns exactly those two from passed to skipped with the parser's name in the skip reason, and that every other test keeps its outcome and reason

The last step of the `ci.yml` job `test`, named `Built wheel runs outside the checkout (one Python version)`, holds only the keys `name`, `if` and `run`. Its `if` is `matrix.python-version == '3.12'`, one version of the matrix, as the pandas step: the wheel is pure Python, so one version shows what it carries, and 3.12 stays in the matrix whichever way its oldest and newest versions move. Its `run` block is, in order: `python -m pip wheel . --no-deps -w "$RUNNER_TEMP/dist"`, so pip's build isolation installs the `[build-system]` requirement and builds the wheel a user's pip would build; `python -m venv "$RUNNER_TEMP/wheel-venv"`, with no system site packages, so the editable install of the earlier steps is not visible in it; that venv's pip installing `"$RUNNER_TEMP"/dist/*.whl`; `cd "$RUNNER_TEMP"`, out of the checkout; that venv's `model-routing demo --out "$RUNNER_TEMP/wheel-demo"`; and that venv's Python reading a standard-library check from a quoted heredoc. README: `## Quickstart` gains one paragraph right after its first `bash` block, saying how another project installs the package, `pip install "<name> @ git+<clone URL>@<commit>"` with `<name>` the `[project]` name in `pyproject.toml`, `<clone URL>` the URL of that block's `git clone` line and a full commit SHA for `<commit>`, and what the CI step checks; and the `## Layout` block names `py.typed` (the v1.13 sub-bullet below). ## 4. Data model

### 4.1 Model and Registry (`registry.py`)
- `@dataclass(frozen=True) class Model`: `id: str`, `family: str`, `price_in: float` (USD per 1M input tokens), `price_out: float` (USD per 1M output tokens), `context_window: int`, `aliases: dict[str, str]` (default empty; provider name to that provider's model ID), and from v1.15 `price_valid_until: str | None` (default `None`)
- v1.15 `price_valid_until` is the last day, inclusive, on which the vendor states the list price, as an ISO date string `YYYY-MM-DD` (four, two and two ASCII digits joined by hyphens, naming a day that exists). Any other value, including a `datetime.date` object, another date spelling or an impossible day such as `2026-02-30`, raises `ValueError` at construction. It is kept as a string so `dataclasses.asdict(model)` stays JSON-able and round-trips through `Registry.load`
- v1.15 `Model.price_expired(today) -> bool` is `True` exactly when `price_valid_until` is set and `today` is a later day; on the stated day itself the price is still valid. `today` is a `datetime.date`, and a `datetime.datetime` counts as its own date; any other type raises `TypeError`
- `Model.cost(input_tokens: int, output_tokens: int) -> float` returns `(input_tokens * price_in + output_tokens * price_out) / 1_000_000`; from v1.212 it prices one call, with the prices of that call's tier (below), which are `price_in` and `price_out` on a model without tiers; from v1.587 it also takes a call's cached reads and cache writes, two keyword-only counts that default to 0 (4.1 v1.587)
- v1.212 `@dataclass(frozen=True) class PriceTier`: `above_input_tokens: int`, `price_in: float`, `price_out: float` (USD per 1M tokens), the prices a call pays when its input is over `above_input_tokens` tokens. `above_input_tokens` is an int that is not a bool and is `>= 1`; each price is an int or a float that is not a bool, is finite and is `>= 0`, and is stored as a float; anything else raises `ValueError` at construction. `model_routing.__all__` gains `PriceTier`
- v1.212 `Model.price_tiers: tuple[PriceTier, ...]`, default `()`, the last field until v1.572 adds `variant` after it, so every positional construction of v1.211 keeps its meaning: a tuple (a list is refused, so a frozen model's tiers cannot change after its checks) of `PriceTier` whose `above_input_tokens` rise strictly and are each below `context_window`, since a tier that no call can reach is a data error; anything else raises `ValueError` at construction
- v1.212 the tier of a call: `Model.cost` prices one call. Its tier is the last of `price_tiers` whose `above_input_tokens` is below the call's `input_tokens`, and the call pays that tier's `price_in` on all of its input tokens and its `price_out` on all of its output tokens, as the two vendor pages of section 9 state ("for the full request"; "each request is priced on its own"); a call at or under every threshold pays `price_in` and `price_out`. So on a model without tiers every cost is the v1.211 one bit for bit, and `Model.cost` is linear only up to a model's first threshold
- v1.455 where a tier's rates come from (row P4): a tier holds rates its vendor page gives, in its text or, where the text says only that long prompts pay other rates, in the price data the page embeds. Such data is read from the object whose model name field is exactly the row's model and whose base prices, in the data's units, are the page's visible prices, so that match fixes the unit before a tier's rate is read; an object of the same name whose base prices differ from the visible ones is not read, and the objects read must give the same tier rates. The `xai/grok-4.7` tier is read this way (9 v1.455)
- v1.212 `Model.base_cost(input_tokens, output_tokens) -> float` returns the v1.211 formula at `price_in` and `price_out` whatever the tiers: the linear price that a total of several calls or a token increment needs, since neither has one call's size (13.2, 13.9). It equals `Model.cost` on a model without tiers. From v1.219 13.2 uses it only for the terms of a model without tiers, and 13.9 for every held-out cost until v1.222, from which 13.9 too uses it only for a model without tiers (13.9 v1.222)
- v1.212 who prices one call: the router at the 5.2 sizes (the rounded-up measured mean, else the task's expected sizes, so the tier is that of one call of those sizes, not a mean of the calls' tiers), the executor on each attempt's completion counts (7), `evaluate` on a token-form row (12.1, one call per row) and the demo (11) call `Model.cost`. A task whose line is a whole conversation (9 v1.90) is priced as one call of the conversation's summed sizes, so a tiered model can be priced at its long-prompt tier although each of its calls is shorter, an over-statement, as rule 5 of 5.2 is stricter there. The delegation formulas of 13.2 and 13.9 price every term with `Model.base_cost`, the totals of K calls and the re-read increments and, with K = 1, a path's one work call too (v1.214), so on a tiered model they stay at the base prices, an under-statement for long contexts that README Limitations states
- v1.219 the inline-or-delegate decision prices a tiered model per call: each work call and each shared parent call of 13.2 at its own tier (13.2 v1.219), so with K = 1 the delegate is charged the cost its `select` ranks it at; the 13.9 held-out costs used `Model.base_cost` until v1.222, which prices them per call in the same way (13.9 v1.222)
- `class Registry`: `Registry(models: Iterable[Model])`; `Registry.load(path) -> Registry` reads the models.json format (section 9); `.models -> tuple[Model, ...]` in file order; `.get(model_id) -> Model` raises `KeyError` for an unknown ID; duplicate IDs raise `ValueError` at construction
- v1.15 `Registry.load` reads the optional `price_valid_until` key of a row (absent or `null` means `None`; an invalid value raises `ValueError` naming the file, as any invalid row does), and `Registry.expired_prices(today) -> tuple[Model, ...]` returns the models whose `price_expired(today)` is true, in file order
- v1.212 `Registry.load` reads the optional `price_tiers` key of a row: absent or `null` means `()`; otherwise a list of objects, each with the keys `above_input_tokens`, `price_in` and `price_out` (other keys are ignored, as on a row), kept in file order; a value of another type, a missing key, or a tier or tier list that 4.1 refuses raises `ValueError` naming the file, as any invalid row does. `dataclasses.asdict(model)` gives each tier as an object with those three keys, so a model with tiers round-trips through `Registry.load` as one without does
- v1.572 variants (row VAR1a): `@dataclass(frozen=True) class Variant`: `name: str`, `reasoning_effort: str | None = None`, `harness: str | None = None` and `context_policy: Mapping[str, str | int | float | bool | None]` (default an empty dict). `name` matches `[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*`, so it holds no `@`, `/` or space; `reasoning_effort` (the effort the runs used, for example `medium`) and `harness` (the agent harness, a name and version) are each `None` or a non-empty `str`; `context_policy` (for example `{"compact_at_tokens": 400000}`) is a mapping whose keys are non-empty `str` and whose values are each `None`, a `bool`, an `int`, a finite `float` or a `str`, stored as a new dict. Anything else raises `ValueError` at construction. The three settings label how the caller's harness ran the model: the library sets no effort from them and compacts nothing (from v1.574 a variant's `provider_options`, which may hold an effort parameter, are sent, 4.1 v1.574). `model_routing.__all__` gains `Variant`
- v1.572 `Model.variant: Variant | None`, default `None`, the last field until v1.581 adds `pricing_basis` after it, after `price_tiers`, so every positional construction of v1.571 keeps its meaning. With a variant, `id` is a `str` `<base>@<variant.name>` with `<base>` non-empty and holding no `@`; any other `id`, or a `variant` that is neither `None` nor a `Variant`, raises `ValueError` at construction. Without one, `id` is checked as in v1.571, so it may hold `@`, as a cascade ID `<cheap>><strong>@<signal>` (7 v1.532) does, and it is no variant route. `Model.base_id` is `<base>` for a model with a variant and `id` otherwise. A model's `id` is its route ID: `Stats` (4.3), every `Candidate` and `RouteDecision` (5) and every log record (8.1) name it, so a variant's runs never pool with its base's or another variant's. `dataclasses.asdict(model)` gains the key `variant`, `None` or an object of the four fields. A `Variant` holds a dict, so, like a `Model` through `aliases`, it is not hashable
- v1.572 `Registry.load` reads the optional `variants` key of a row: absent or `null` means none; otherwise an object that maps each variant name to an object whose keys are among `reasoning_effort`, `harness` and `context_policy`, a `null` value meaning the key is absent, as on a row. Unlike a row, a variant object refuses any other key, so a misspelt setting, or `items_per_call` and `provider_options` before rows VAR1c and VAR1d, never routes as its base. A `variants` or variant value of another type, a refused key, a variant that 4.1 refuses, and a row whose `id` holds `@`, with or without `variants`, raise `ValueError` naming the file, as any invalid row does. Each variant becomes a `Model` with `id` `<row id>@<name>`, the row's `family`, prices, `context_window`, `aliases` (a copy), `price_valid_until` and `price_tiers`, and that `variant`, placed right after its base in the object's order; the base stays a route, with no variant. So a variant is priced at its base's list prices and fits its base's window, and differs by its own stats, and so its own 5.2 sizes. The duplicate check above keeps route IDs unique, and a model with a variant written as a row by `asdict` is refused for its `id`: its base's row with `variants` holds it
- v1.573 items per call (row VAR1c): `Variant` gains a last field, `items_per_call: int = 1`, after `context_policy`, so a variant built with positional arguments keeps its meaning: how many items one call of the route handles, for example the answers or the criteria a judge grades in one call. It is an `int` of at least 1 that is not a `bool`, else `ValueError` at construction. `Model.items_per_call` is its variant's `items_per_call`, and 1 for a model without a variant, so a base is always 1. `Registry.load` reads `items_per_call` in a variant object, a null meaning absent as for the other settings, so v1.572's refusal of the key ends; `provider_options` was still refused then, until row VAR1d (v1.574). `dataclasses.asdict(model)` gives a variant with `items_per_call` as its last key. The library never batches items: the caller's harness puts k items in one call, and the route is measured per item (4.3) and priced per item once measured (5.2)
- v1.574 provider options (row VAR1d): `Variant` gains a last field, `provider_options: Mapping[str, object]` (default an empty dict), after `items_per_call`, so a variant built with positional arguments keeps its meaning: request settings that the executor sends to the provider on each call of the route (6, 7), for example `{"reasoning_effort": "high"}`, the effort parameter of an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. It is a mapping whose keys are non-empty `str` and whose values are JSON values: `None`, a `bool`, an `int`, a finite `float`, a `str`, a list or tuple of JSON values, or a mapping of `str` keys to JSON values. It is stored as a new dict, each mapping in it as a new dict and each list or tuple as a new list, so a later change to what the caller passed never reaches the route; anything else raises `ValueError` at construction. `Model.provider_options` is a new copy, in that stored form, of its variant's `provider_options` on each read, and an empty dict for a model without a variant, so a base sends none. `Registry.load` reads `provider_options` in a variant object, a null meaning absent as for the other settings, so the refusal of v1.572 and v1.573 ends and a variant object refuses only keys outside its five settings. `dataclasses.asdict(model)` gives a variant with `provider_options` as its last key. `reasoning_effort` stays a label of the effort the runs used, while `provider_options` is sent; the library checks no agreement between the two, and either way the route's stats are its own (4.3)
- v1.581 self-hosted pricing (row SELF1a): `Model` gains a last field, `pricing_basis: str = "list"`, after `variant`, so every positional construction of v1.580 keeps its meaning: `"list"`, prices read from a vendor's page, or `"self_hosted"`, prices derived from what an hour of the caller's own serving costs. Any other value raises `ValueError` at construction, and so does a `self_hosted` model with price tiers, since an hour costs the same whatever a prompt's length. `self_hosted_prices(usd_per_hour, tokens_per_hour_in, tokens_per_hour_out, utilization, input_cost_share) -> tuple[float, float]` returns `(price_in, price_out)` in USD per 1M tokens: `price_in = usd_per_hour * input_cost_share / (tokens_per_hour_in * utilization) * 1_000_000` and `price_out = usd_per_hour * (1 - input_cost_share) / (tokens_per_hour_out * utilization) * 1_000_000`, so an hour fully used at those throughputs is charged once, its input share on input tokens and the rest on output tokens, and the routing math of 5.2 is unchanged. Each argument is an int or a float that is not a bool and is finite; `usd_per_hour` is at least 0, each throughput (the tokens one serving unit reads, or writes, in an hour of full use on this work) is above 0, `utilization` (the share of the hour the unit spends on this work) is in (0, 1] and `input_cost_share` (the share of the hour charged to input) is in [0, 1]; anything else raises `ValueError` naming the argument, an int too large for a float included. So does a derived price that is not a finite float, naming that price, as inputs this large or this small can give (an hour of 1e308 USD at a throughput of 1, or a throughput and utilization whose product underflows to 0), since such a price could never be ranked (review iter-428 must-fix 2). The throughputs describe one workload, and the split of an hour between input and output is an approximation the caller chooses: a unit that reads and writes in the same hour has no one price per token of each. For example 10 USD an hour, 36,000,000 input and 2,000,000 output tokens an hour, utilization 0.5 and share 0.5 give 0.2778 and 5.0 to four places. `model_routing.__all__` gains `self_hosted_prices` after `Variant`. Selection, execution, records and reports read `price_in` and `price_out` as for any model, so a self-hosted model is routed by its measured success at its derived price and nothing else of v1.580 changes; `dataclasses.asdict(model)` gains `pricing_basis` as its last key
- v1.581 `Registry.load` reads the optional `pricing_basis` key of a row, once the row is checked to be an object (any other row raises `ValueError` naming the file, as before v1.581; review iter-428 must-fix 1): absent or `null` is `list`, so every row of v1.580 loads as before, and a value other than `list` and `self_hosted` raises. A `self_hosted` row holds the five keys `usd_per_hour`, `tokens_per_hour_in`, `tokens_per_hour_out`, `utilization` and `input_cost_share`, none `null`, and no `price_in`, `price_out` or `price_tiers` key, since its prices are derived: they are `self_hosted_prices` of the five, and `price_valid_until` may still state the last day of the hourly rate, a reserved term's end for example. A `list` row holding any of the five keys raises, so a row that names an hourly cost but not its basis never routes at a list price unnoticed: the one exception to a row's extra keys being ignored. Each refusal, and a value that `self_hosted_prices` refuses, raises `ValueError` naming the file, as any invalid row does. A row's variants keep its basis and its derived prices. A `list` model written as a row by `asdict` loads back as itself; a `self_hosted` one is refused, since it holds derived prices and none of the five keys: its source row holds them, as a variant's base row holds the variant (v1.572)
- v1.582 deployment and base (row SELF1b): `Model` gains two last fields after `pricing_basis`, until v1.586 adds `scope_tasks` after them, `deployment: str | None = None` and then `base_model: str | None = None`, so every positional construction of v1.581 keeps its meaning. `deployment` says where the model runs: `"api"`, a vendor's endpoint, or `"self_hosted"`, weights the caller serves. `None` at construction becomes `"self_hosted"` when `pricing_basis` is `"self_hosted"` and `"api"` otherwise, so every list-priced model of v1.581 is `api`, the row's default, and a v1.581 self-hosted model is not read as a vendor's; any other value raises `ValueError` at construction. Either deployment goes with either basis: open weights the caller serves may be charged at a vendor's list price for them (`self_hosted`, `list`), and capacity a vendor rents by the hour behind its own endpoint may be priced from that hour (`api`, `self_hosted`). It is a label: no rule of 5, 7 or 13 reads it. `base_model` names the base of a fine-tune: `None`, or a non-empty `str`, else `ValueError` at construction. `Registry(models)` checks each model whose `base_model` is set, after the duplicate check, in this order: its base is not the model itself (its `base_id`), is a model of the same registry, is no variant (a fine-tune changes weights, not a setup, so it names the base's row) and names no `base_model` itself (no chain), and the model's `family` is the base's; anything else raises `ValueError`. So a fine-tune is its base's family, and every reader of `family` reads it so: rules 2 and 4 of 5.2 (`exclude_families` and generator isolation), the parent check of 13.4, the records' `family` key (7, 8.1) and `report` by `family` (8.3). Why: a fine-tune starts from its base's weights, so as a judge it can keep the base family's preference for that family's outputs, the self-preference that `independent_of_generator` is there to avoid, whatever family name its owner would give it. A variant of a fine-tune keeps both fields, as it keeps the basis: `Registry.load` writes every field of a variant from its base row, and from v1.583 `Registry` checks a directly built variant against its base's model (4.1 v1.583). `dataclasses.asdict(model)` gains `deployment`, resolved, and `base_model` as its last two keys
- v1.582 `Registry.load` reads the optional `deployment` and `base_model` keys of a row, absent or `null` meaning `None`. A row with a `base_model` may leave out `family` (absent or `null`): it then has the `family` of the row whose `id` is its `base_model`, before it or after it in the file, and with no such row, or one whose own `family` is absent or `null`, it raises. A stated `family` other than the base's raises by the registry check. Each refusal, the registry's checks included, raises `ValueError` naming the file, so from v1.582 a duplicate ID in a loaded file names the file too. A row's variants keep its `deployment` and `base_model`, and a list-priced model written as a row by `asdict`, a fine-tune included, loads back as itself
- v1.583 a variant agrees with its base (row VAR2, review iter-429 should-fix 4): after the base checks of v1.582, `Registry(models)` checks, in the registry's order, each model with a `variant` whose `base_id` is the `id` of a model of the same registry: its `family`, `pricing_basis`, `deployment` (as resolved at construction) and `base_model` must each equal that model's, and otherwise it raises `ValueError` naming the variant, its base model and, in that order, each field that differs, with the variant's value and the base's. Why: rules 2 and 4 of 5.2 and the parent check of 13.4 read a variant's own `family` as its base's (v1.572, v1.582; review iter-431 nit 3), which only `Registry.load` ensured, by writing every field of a variant from its base row, so a variant built directly, such as `Model("acme/ft@high", "acme", ..., variant=Variant("high"))` beside a fine-tune `acme/ft` of `v/base`, could judge the output of `v/base` under a family its base does not have; and `pricing_basis` and `deployment` say how the base is priced and where it runs, which a setup of it does not change. A loaded variant always passes, since its fields are its base row's. The duplicate check comes first and the base checks next, so a variant whose own `base_model` names itself or no model of the registry gets v1.582's message. A variant whose base is no model of the registry is not checked, as v1.572 lets a caller route such a variant alone (for example `v/d@batch4` without `v/d`). A directly built variant's prices, `price_tiers`, `price_valid_until`, `context_window` and `aliases` stay free: a setup sent in `provider_options` may be billed at other rates or open another window, a batch or a long-context setting for example, which only its caller can state, and 5.2 and 7 read that variant's own values; `Registry.load` still writes them from the base row, so no loaded variant differs from its base in them. Without a directly built variant that differs from its base in one of the four checked fields, every registry, route and decision is v1.582's
- v1.586 task scope (row SCOPE1): `Model` gains a last field, `scope_tasks: tuple[str, ...] = ()`, after `base_model`, until v1.587 adds the two cache prices after it, so every positional construction of v1.585 keeps its meaning: the tasks the model was built and measured for, each a task name or a glob pattern as `fnmatch.fnmatchcase` reads it (`*`, `?` and `[...]`, case-sensitive, so a pattern without them names one task). `()` scopes the model to no task in particular: it is a candidate on every task, as every model of v1.585 is. A value other than a tuple of non-empty `str` raises `ValueError` at construction, a list included, so a frozen model's scope cannot change after its checks, as with `price_tiers`; a repeated pattern is kept and matches as one. Rule 5a of 5.2 is the only rule that reads it. `dataclasses.asdict(model)` gains `scope_tasks` as its last key, a tuple that `json` writes as a list. Why: a model trained for one job, such as a fine-tune exposed as a tool for one task, can be cheap and over the bar there while it was never measured elsewhere, and its gains can differ by domain; without a scope, cold start (rule 6 and the `best_available` and prior orders of 5.3) could send it the calls of a task it was not built for before any measurement exists. A variant built by `Registry.load` keeps its base row's scope; a directly built variant's scope stays free, as its prices do (v1.583 checks four fields), since a setup may serve fewer tasks than its base
- v1.586 `Registry.load` reads the optional `scope_tasks` key of a row: absent, `null` or an empty list is `()`, and otherwise a list of non-empty strings, kept in file order as a tuple; any other value, a string included, raises `ValueError` naming the file, as any invalid row does. A row's variants keep its scope. A list-priced model with no variant written as a row by `asdict` loads back as itself, scoped or not, an unscoped one holding `[]` (a self-hosted model or a variant is refused as before v1.586: its source row holds it, 4.1 v1.572 and v1.581); so an empty list means every task, and a model kept off every task is a row left out of the file
- v1.587 cache prices (row CACHE1a): `Model` gains two last fields after `scope_tasks`, `price_cached_in: float | None = None` and then `price_cache_write: float | None = None`, so every positional construction of v1.586 keeps its meaning: USD per 1M input tokens that the provider serves from its prompt cache (a cached read) and that it writes to the cache (a cache write), as a vendor page lists them beside its input price. Each is `None`, the price unknown, or an int or a float that is not a bool, is finite and is `>= 0`, stored as a float; anything else raises `ValueError` at construction naming the field. A model with `price_tiers` holding either raises `ValueError`, since a vendor that charges long prompts more may charge their cached reads more too and one cache price would then under-state them, so a tiered model's reads and writes are priced at its call's tier input price; so does a `self_hosted` model holding either, since an hour's throughputs already hold whatever caching its serving did (4.1 v1.581). `dataclasses.asdict(model)` gains both as its last two keys
- v1.587 `Model.cost(input_tokens, output_tokens, *, cached_input_tokens=0, cache_write_tokens=0)`: `input_tokens` counts every input token of the call, its cached reads and cache writes included, as an OpenAI-compatible `usage.prompt_tokens` includes its `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`. Each count is an int that is not a bool and is `>= 0`, and their sum is at most `input_tokens`; anything else raises `ValueError` naming the count, or both counts for the sum. The call's tier is the one its `input_tokens` selects (v1.212). With `p_in` and `p_out` that tier's prices, and `r` and `w` the `price_cached_in` and `price_cache_write`, each `p_in` when `None`, the cost is `((input_tokens - cached_input_tokens - cache_write_tokens) * p_in + cached_input_tokens * r + cache_write_tokens * w + output_tokens * p_out) / 1_000_000`. With both counts 0 it is computed as v1.586's `(input_tokens * p_in + output_tokens * p_out) / 1_000_000`, so bit for bit, and a call is priced as a cache hit only when its counts say so: a repeated prompt is never assumed to hit. A write premium can make caching lose: at `price_in` 3, `price_cached_in` 0.3, `price_cache_write` 3.75 and `price_out` 15, a call of 10,000 input and 500 output tokens costs 0.0375 uncached, 0.0132 with 9,000 cached reads, and 0.04425 with 9,000 cache writes and no read, as the first and only call of a one-shot prompt pays; and a model at `price_in` 2 and `price_out` 15 that never hits costs 0.0275 on that call, more than the pricier model at 90% reads. `Model.base_cost` is unchanged. In v1.587 no package module passes either count, so every route (5), record (7, 8.1), report (8.3), delegation decision (13), evidence file and README transcript is v1.586's; measured counts per task and route in routing are row CACHE1b (done in v1.588, 4.3 and 5.2), and the attempt records' counts row CACHE1c (done in v1.589, 7 and 8.1)
- v1.587 `Registry.load` reads the optional `price_cached_in` and `price_cache_write` keys of a row, absent or `null` meaning `None`, each value passed to `Model` as it is, so a string or a bool raises rather than being read as a number; a refusal raises `ValueError` naming the file, as any invalid row does. A `self_hosted` row holding either key raises, as it refuses `price_in` (v1.581). A row's variants keep both. A list-priced model with no variant written as a row by `asdict` loads back as itself, with or without cache prices
- v1.622 regions and data retention (row POL1a): `Model` gains two last fields after `price_cache_write`, so every positional construction of v1.621 keeps its meaning: `regions: tuple[str, ...] = ()`, the regions in which the caller's calls of the model are served, `()` meaning none stated, and `zero_data_retention: bool | None = None`, whether the provider keeps no prompt or output of the caller's calls once each ends, `None` meaning not stated. `regions` is a tuple of non-empty `str` (a list is refused, so a frozen model's regions cannot change, as with `scope_tasks`), kept in its order with any repeat, and `zero_data_retention` is `None` or a `bool`; anything else raises `ValueError` at construction. Both are what the registry's owner states about its own account with a provider, not a certification: the library checks no provider and reads them only for a `Policy` (5.1 and 5.2 v1.622). `Registry.load` reads the optional `regions` key of a row, absent or `null` meaning `()`, else a list stored as a tuple (any other value is refused, so a string is never read as its characters), and the optional `zero_data_retention` key, absent or `null` meaning `None`, its value passed to `Model` as it is, so `"yes"` or `1` raises; a refusal raises `ValueError` naming the file, as any invalid row does. A row's variants have its row's values, since `Registry.load` builds each from its row, while a fine-tune row (v1.582) takes neither from its base row, though it takes its family from it, since it may be served apart from its base, so a fine-tune row that leaves them out states none; and `dataclasses.asdict(model)` gives `regions` as a tuple, which `json.dumps` writes as a list, so a model round-trips through `Registry.load`. The shipped models.json states neither key, so every shipped model has `()` and `None`

### 4.2 Task (`tasks.py`)
- `@dataclass(frozen=True) class Task` fields and defaults:
  - `name: str`
  - `bar: float` (required, in [0, 1]; the minimum acceptable success rate against the task's acceptance check, for a judge its agreement with gold labels)
  - `min_samples: int = 30` (fewer measured trials than this can never clear the bar)
  - `confidence: float = 0.95`
  - `independent_of_generator: bool = True` (exclude the generator's model AND its family when the caller names a `generator_model`; no effect otherwise)
  - `exclude_families: tuple[str, ...] = ()`
  - `expected_input_tokens: int = 1000`, `expected_output_tokens: int = 200`
  - `on_no_model: str = "refuse"` (or `"best_available"`)
  - `max_fallbacks: int = 2`
  - `prior_category: str | None = None`
  - `timeout_s: float = 60.0`
  - v1.201 `fallback_below_bar: bool = False` (when some model clears the bar, the fallbacks go on below it, 5.3); the last field until v1.511 adds `slices` after it (below), so a task built with positional arguments keeps its meaning
- Invalid values raise `ValueError` at construction: bar outside [0, 1], `min_samples < 1`, confidence outside (0, 1), unknown `on_no_model`, negative token counts or `max_fallbacks`
- v1.201 `fallback_below_bar` must be a bool (`type(value) is bool`), so `1`, `0`, `"true"` and `None` raise `ValueError` at construction; `load_tasks` reads it from a JSON `true` or `false`, and a row without it gets `False`, so every packaged task (9) keeps it off
- `load_tasks(path) -> dict[str, Task]` reads `{"tasks": [ {field: value, ...}, ... ]}`; JSON lists become tuples; duplicate names raise `ValueError`
- v1.511 slices (row STRAT1): `Task` gains a last field, `slices: Mapping[str, Mapping[str, number]]`, default an empty dict, after `fallback_below_bar`, so a task built with positional arguments keeps its meaning. A slice is a part of the task's items that a call names before it is routed (5.2); each key is a slice name, and each value gives that slice its own `bar`, `min_samples`, `expected_input_tokens` or `expected_output_tokens`, any of them or none, every value it does not give coming from the task. A slice name is a non-empty `str` that holds no `@`; `bar` is a finite real number in [0, 1], `min_samples` an `int` of at least 1 and each token count an `int` of at least 0, none of them a `bool`. Any other key, a value of another type or out of range, a `slices` or slice value that is not a mapping, and any slice on a task whose name holds `@` raise `ValueError` naming the task at construction. The constructor stores a copy (a new dict of new dicts), so a later change to the caller's mapping changes no task, and `slices` is compared but not hashed, so a `Task` stays hashable. `load_tasks` reads it from a JSON object such as `"slices": {"deep": {"bar": 0.9}}`, and a row without it gets `{}`, so no packaged task has a slice. The demo's tasks file (11) holds the key only for a task whose `slices` is not empty, so the files `run_demo` writes other than `calls.jsonl` keep their bytes

- v1.535 cascades (row ESC2a): `Task` gains a last field, `cascades`, after `slices`, and `load_tasks` reads it; the contract is 7 v1.532 and v1.535
- v1.567 failure policy (row CPS1a): `Task` gains a last field, `failure_policy: str = "none"`, after `cascades`, so a task built with positional arguments keeps its meaning. It says what the caller does when a call's result fails the task's acceptance check: `"none"`, the default, prices nothing for it, and `"retry_same"` says the caller runs the work again on the same route until it succeeds, so 5.3 ranks the routes that clear the bar by expected cost per success. The library runs no retry itself: `Executor.call` (7) tries the primary and then the fallbacks as before. Any other value, one that is not a `str` included, raises `ValueError` naming the task at construction. `load_tasks` reads it from a JSON string and a row without it gets `"none"`; a slice (v1.511) has no key of its own and takes the task's; the demo's tasks file (11) holds the key only when it is not `"none"`, so no packaged task has it and the files `run_demo` writes keep their bytes
- v1.607 shadow fields (row CANARY1a): `Task` gains two last fields, after `failure_policy`, so a task built with positional arguments keeps its meaning: `shadow_rate: float = 0.0`, the share of the task's `.call`s also sent to a shadow route (7 v1.607), a finite `int` or `float` in [0, 1] that is not a `bool`; and `shadow_route: str | None = None`, the model ID of that route, None for the default route 7 v1.607 names, else a non-empty `str`. Any other value raises `ValueError` naming the task at construction; whether a `shadow_route` is in the registry is checked by `.call` (7), since a task holds no registry. `load_tasks` reads them from a JSON number and a JSON string or `null`, and a row without them gets the defaults; a slice (v1.511) has no key of its own and takes the task's; the demo's tasks file (11) holds each key only when it is not its default, so no packaged task has them and the files `run_demo` writes keep their bytes
- v1.628 latency bar (row LAT1b): `Task` gains two last fields, after `shadow_route`, so a task built with positional arguments keeps its meaning: `max_p95_ms: float | None = None`, the highest 95th-percentile time in milliseconds a route may take on the task's calls (5.2 v1.628), None for no bar, else a finite `int` or `float` above 0 that is not a `bool`; and `latency_unknown: str = "allow"`, what 5.2 rule 5f does with a route whose time is unknown, `"allow"` or `"deny"`, which has no effect without a bar. Any other value, one that is not a `str` included, raises `ValueError` naming the task at construction. `load_tasks` reads them from a JSON number or `null` and a JSON string, and a row without them gets the defaults; a slice (v1.511) has no key of its own and takes the task's, judged on its own key's times (5.2 v1.628); the demo's tasks file (11) holds each key only when it is not its default, so no packaged task has them and the files `run_demo` writes keep their bytes

### 4.3 Quality statistics (`stats.py`)
- `wilson_lower_bound(successes: int, trials: int, confidence: float = 0.95) -> float`
  - z = `NormalDist().inv_cdf(1 - (1 - confidence) / 2)` (two-sided interval, lower end); p = successes / trials
  - LB = `(p + z*z/(2n) - z*sqrt(p*(1-p)/n + z*z/(4n*n))) / (1 + z*z/n)`, clamped to `>= 0.0`
  - returns `0.0` when `trials == 0`; raises `ValueError` when `successes < 0`, `trials < 0` or `successes > trials`
  - v1.568 (row CI29): returns exactly `0.0` when `successes == 0`, the formula's exact value there for a confidence in [0, 1) (with `p` 0 and `z >= 0` its two terms cancel), after the same checks and the same `z`, so every error is unchanged. Computed in floating point the two terms can leave a residue of about 1e-17 whose sign can turn on the last bits of `z`, and so can differ by platform: the clamp turns a negative residue into 0.0 and keeps a positive one. Observed: at 0.95 `(0, 10)` was 0.0 on the machine that wrote 5.3 v1.567's tests and about 2.0e-17 on the CI runners, so the per-success estimate was `None` on the first and finite on the second; that machine keeps a positive residue at `(0, 15)`. Two candidates at 0 successes now tie on `quality_lb`, so each order of 5.3 and each comparison of 13.5 falls to its next term, never to a residue. Every bound at 1 or more successes is unchanged, bit for bit
  - reference values at confidence 0.95 (to 6 decimals): (27, 30) 0.743789; (45, 50) 0.786398; (90, 100) 0.825634; (170, 200) 0.793944; (10, 10) 0.722467; (0, 10) 0.0
  - v1.592 (row CI31): `z` itself can differ in its last bit by platform, since `NormalDist().inv_cdf` may use the platform's floating-point library and fused operations. Observed: at 0.95 it is 1.9599639845400534 on the machine that wrote 5.2 v1.591's tests and 1.9599639845400536 on the CI runners, and so a bound at 1 or more successes (for example (37, 40)) can differ in its last bit between them, while on one platform every bound is fixed. A test that pins a decision's bytes across platforms therefore rounds each `quality_lb` to 12 decimals first (tests/test_cache_cascades.py); every other value it pins is exact
  - v1.593 (row CI32): every test that hashes a decision or an evaluation's result hashes it through one helper, tests/decision_hash.py, whose `decision_sha256` rounds each float under `quality_lb`, `parent_quality_lb`, `delegate_quality_lb` and `expected_cost_per_success_usd` (a bound, or a value divided by one) to 12 decimals and hashes every other value exact, so a value without those keys keeps its hash. The demo's decision pins of 5.1 v1.535 and v1.576 (tests/test_cascade_candidates.py, tests/test_procedure_routing.py) hashed bounds at 1 or more successes that were equal under both values of `z` by their counts alone; they are recomputed through the helper at those versions (bfad91b and 2f8de0b), the same there and at v1.593 under both values, and a test checks each under both. tests/test_decision_hash_pins.py fails when a test file hashes a JSON value in one expression (`sha256(json.dumps(`) without the helper, unless that site is on its list of the four that hold no bound or hash the exact bytes on purpose
- `class Stats`: in-memory map from `(task, model_id)` to `(successes, trials)`
  - `Stats()`; `.get(task, model_id) -> tuple[int, int]` returns `(0, 0)` when absent; `.add(task, model_id, successes, trials)` accumulates (adds to existing counts) and validates like `wilson_lower_bound`
  - `Stats.load(path)` and `.save(path)` use `{"stats": [{"task": ..., "model": ..., "successes": int, "trials": int}, ...]}`; save writes rows sorted by (task, model)
  - `.merge(other: Stats) -> Stats` returns a new Stats with summed counts
- `calibrate_from_results(rows: Iterable[dict]) -> Stats`: each row has `task`, `model`, and either `correct` (bool) or both `prediction` and `gold` (correct when equal with `==`); a row with neither raises `ValueError`. Each row is one trial
- v1.1 validation: `correct` must be a real boolean (`type(correct) is bool`); a string such as `"false"`, a number or null raises `ValueError`. A row that is not a dict raises `ValueError`. `Stats.load` requires `successes` and `trials` to be integers that are not booleans (`isinstance(v, int) and not isinstance(v, bool)`); floats such as `30.9`, strings and booleans raise `ValueError`, never truncation
- v1.33 measured token counts: `Stats` also holds, per `(task, model_id)`, optional token totals: `input_tokens` and `output_tokens`, the summed input and output tokens of `token_trials` of its trials, the calls whose token counts were recorded. A key with none has all three at 0. Token totals only come with trials, so `0 <= token_trials <= trials` always holds, and a model with token totals is measured (`trials > 0`, 5.3)
- v1.33 `.add(task, model_id, successes, trials, *, input_tokens=None, output_tokens=None, token_trials=None)`: `input_tokens` and `output_tokens` are given together or not at all. Given, each is an integer `>= 0` that is not a bool, and they are totals over `token_trials` of this call's `trials`; `token_trials` defaults to `trials` and must be an integer that is not a bool with `1 <= token_trials <= trials`, so tokens cannot come with zero trials. One total without the other, `token_trials` without the totals, or any invalid value raises `ValueError`, and nothing is added when `add` raises
- v1.33 `.tokens(task, model_id) -> tuple[int, int, int]` returns `(input_tokens, output_tokens, token_trials)`, `(0, 0, 0)` when none are recorded. `.mean_tokens(task, model_id) -> tuple[int, int] | None` returns the mean input and output tokens per recorded call, each rounded up to an integer in integer arithmetic (`-(-total // token_trials)`, never through a float), or `None` when `token_trials` is 0. Rounding up means a model without price tiers is never priced below the mean list cost of its recorded calls (`Model.cost` is linear in the token counts on such a model; from v1.212 a model with `price_tiers` is priced as one call of the rounded-up mean sizes, at that call's tier, 4.1), though one call may cost more than its mean; integers keep `Model.cost` on whole token counts, as everywhere else
- v1.33 `.merge` sums the token totals and `token_trials` as it sums the counts. `.get` and `.items()` are unchanged and carry no tokens
- v1.33 files: a `Stats.load` row may carry `input_tokens`, `output_tokens` and `token_trials`, all three or none. A partial set, a value that is a bool, null or anything but an integer, a negative total, or a `token_trials` outside `1..trials` raises `ValueError` naming the file. Rows for the same key accumulate as before. `.save` writes the three keys, after `trials` and in that order, only for a key with `token_trials > 0`, so a Stats with no token totals saves the bytes v1.32 saves and a v1.32 file loads unchanged
- v1.33 `calibrate_from_results`: a row may carry `input_tokens` and `output_tokens`, both or neither, each an integer `>= 0` that is not a bool (one without the other, null, a float or a string raises `ValueError`, and every row is still validated before the returned Stats exists). A row with them adds one token trial with those counts; a row without them adds a trial with none. The `calibrate` command (10) needs no change: its printed table is unchanged, and the file it writes carries the token keys of the rows that had them
- v1.140 `items_needed(success: float, bar: float, confidence: float = 0.95, max_items: int = 10_000) -> int | None`: how many labelled calibration items a model needs on a task before its Wilson lower bound there clears `bar`, if its success rate on the task is `success`
  - successes at `n` items: `floor(n * s)`, where `s` is the decimal that `repr(float(success))` prints, taken exactly (`fractions.Fraction(repr(float(success)))`; v1.141 adds the `float`), so 0.29 at 100 items gives 29 where floating `0.29 * 100` is `28.999999999999996`; rounding down means a planned count never clears early
  - returns the smallest `n` in `1..max_items` such that every count `m` from `n` through `max_items` gives `wilson_lower_bound(floor(m * s), m, confidence) >= bar`, or `None` when `max_items` itself does not clear. The bound is not monotone in `n` because of the floor: at success 0.9 and bar 0.8 (confidence 0.95), 68 items (61 successes, bound 0.802421) clear but 73 (65 successes, 0.798374) do not, and the answer is 74 (66 successes, 0.800912), the count from which more items at the same rate never fall back below the bar
  - with `bar > 0` the answer is `None` whenever `success <= bar`, since the Wilson lower bound never exceeds the observed rate `floor(n * s) / n <= s` and equals it only at 0 successes; with `bar == 0` every count clears and the answer is 1. With every item right the bound is `n / (n + z*z)`, so at bar 0.9 and confidence 0.95 the answer is `ceil(9 * z*z)`, 35 (`9 * z*z` is 34.573)
  - arguments: `success` and `bar` are finite real numbers that are not bools, in `[0, 1]`; `confidence` is a finite real number that is not a bool, in `(0, 1)` as a `Task` requires (4.2); `max_items` is an integer that is not a bool, `>= 1`; anything else raises `ValueError`. It computes one bound per count from `max_items` down, so its time is linear in `max_items`
  - the count is per model on one task. The router also needs the task's `min_samples` measured trials before it admits a measured model (5.2, step 6), so a plan below `min_samples` still needs `min_samples` items; and in `evaluate` (12) the calibration items are one half of the matrix's items, so a matrix needs about the planned count divided by `calibration_fraction`
- v1.511 a sliced trial (row STRAT1): a slice's counts live in `Stats` under the task key `<task>@<slice>` (for example `support@deep`), so `Stats`, its methods and its file format are v1.510's. `calibrate_from_results` reads an optional `slice` from a row: absent or null is no slice; anything else must be a non-empty `str` that holds no `@`, on a row whose `task` holds no `@`, else `ValueError`, raised before the returned Stats exists as for every row check. A sliced row adds its one trial, with its token counts when it has them, under both `<task>` and `<task>@<slice>`, so the task's pooled counts are those of all its rows whether or not they carry a slice, and a results file without the key gives v1.510's stats bit for bit. The `calibrate` command (10) needs no change: its table lists each slice key as a task

- v1.535 a cascade key (row ESC2a): `Stats` keeps a cascade's escalation count beside its counts, `.add` and `Stats.load` take it, `.save` writes it and `calibrate_from_results` reads a row's `escalated`; the contract is 7 v1.532 and v1.535
- v1.572 a route ID (row VAR1a): `Stats` keys on a model's `id`, a variant's being `<base>@<name>` (4.1), so `Stats`, its methods, its file format and `calibrate_from_results` are v1.571's. Nothing copies counts or token totals from a base to its variants or back, so a variant with no trials of its own is unmeasured (cold start, 5.3) and priced at the task's sizes (5.2)
- v1.573 a trial of a route whose `items_per_call` is k (row VAR1c): one item, a success when that item's own result passes the task's check, carrying the token counts of the whole call that handled it, so `mean_tokens` is the mean of one call (totals added over n calls with `token_trials` n, or over their k times n items with each call's counts once per item, give the same mean). The Wilson bound counts trials as independent, so a candidate is admitted on whole outcomes: the criteria a judge grades for one item, or reruns of one item, are one trial, never several. Items that share a call can still be correlated, which counts cannot show, so a bar cleared by a route with k above 1 assumes they are not (a stated limit). `Stats`, its methods, its file format and `calibrate_from_results` are v1.572's
- v1.577 a procedure key (row PROC1b): a key whose model ID starts with `proc:` is a procedure's route ID (4.5) and must be a valid one, `proc:<name>@<version>` with an optional `+<model>` as `Procedure` allows, else `ValueError`; it is never a cascade key, even when its model holds `>`. Beside its counts it holds `cost_usd`, the summed cost of its trials: per trial its model calls at list price plus its `tool_cost_usd`, as the caller measured them (row PROC1c's records give both). It holds no token totals and no escalations: one trial may make several model calls, so a mean of one call would not price a trial. `.add` takes a keyword `cost_usd`, required for a procedure key and refused for any other: a finite `int` or `float` that is not a `bool`, `>= 0`, stored as a `float`, and 0 when `trials` is 0, so a cost never comes without trials; an `int` too large for a `float` is a `ValueError` too, never an `OverflowError` (review iter-424 should-fix 1); an add whose cost would take the key's sum past the largest `float` raises `ValueError`, so a sum, its mean and a saved file stay finite, and `.merge`, `Stats.load` and `calibrate_from_results`, which add through `.add`, raise it too (review iter-424 must-fix 1); token totals or `escalated` on a procedure key raise `ValueError`, and nothing is added when `add` raises. `.cost(task, model_id) -> float` returns the summed cost, 0.0 when none; `.mean_cost(task, model_id) -> float | None` that sum over the key's trials, None when it has none or is no procedure key. `.merge` sums the costs. `Stats.load`: a procedure row needs `cost_usd`, checked as `.add` checks it, and carries no token keys and no `escalated`; on any other row `cost_usd` is ignored, as every key a row does not use is, so v1.576's files load unchanged. `.save` writes `cost_usd` right after `trials` for each procedure key and for no other, so a Stats without one saves v1.576's bytes. `calibrate_from_results`: a procedure row needs `cost_usd`, its one trial's cost, and carries no token counts and no `escalated`, each else a `ValueError` raised before the returned Stats exists; a sliced one adds its trial and cost under both keys; any other row's `cost_usd` is ignored as before. A stated limit: a registry ID that starts with `proc:` is not refused (4.1 keeps IDs opaque), but its stats key is always read as a procedure key, so its rows need `cost_usd` and hold no token totals, and as a registry candidate it is still priced as a model (5.2), never at that cost; so name no registry model that way (review iter-424 nit 1)
- v1.588 measured cache counts (row CACHE1b): beside its token totals, `Stats` holds per `(task, model_id)` the summed cached reads and cache writes of the trials that reported them, each with its own trial count, since a provider may report one and not the other (an OpenAI-compatible `usage` reports cached reads and no write count). `.add(task, model_id, successes, trials, *, ..., cached_input_tokens=None, cached_trials=None, cache_write_tokens=None, cache_write_trials=None)`: each count is an `int` that is not a `bool` and is `>= 0`, given only with `input_tokens` and `output_tokens`, and is a total over `cached_trials` (or `cache_write_trials`) of this call's token trials, each an `int` from 1 to that `token_trials` and defaulting to it, so a trials argument without its count raises `ValueError`. The counts given sum to at most `input_tokens`, since a call's cached reads and cache writes are input tokens of it (4.1 v1.587); anything else raises `ValueError` naming the count or the trials and adds nothing. A cascade or a procedure key holds no token totals, so a cache count on one raises as a token total does
- v1.588 `.cache_tokens(task, model_id) -> tuple[int, int, int, int]` returns `(cached_input_tokens, cached_trials, cache_write_tokens, cache_write_trials)`, `(0, 0, 0, 0)` when none are recorded. `.mean_cache_tokens(task, model_id) -> tuple[int | None, int | None]` returns the mean cached reads and the mean cache writes per reporting call, each rounded down (integer arithmetic, `//`) and `None` when no trial reported that count, so an unreported count is unknown, never 0: rounded up, a mean could exceed the rounded-up mean input it must fit inside (5.2 v1.588), and rounded down a cached-read mean never over-states the cached share, so the discounted reads never price a route below what its trials support; a cache-write mean rounded down moves under one written token per call to the input price, so a write premium is under-stated by less than one token's price gap (review iter-436 should-fix 1). `.merge` sums the four values as it sums the token totals; `.get`, `.items()` and `.tokens` are unchanged
- v1.588 files: a `Stats.load` row may carry `cached_input_tokens` with `cached_trials`, and `cache_write_tokens` with `cache_write_trials`, each pair both keys or neither and only beside the three token keys, each value an integer as above, so `null`, a bool, a string, a half pair or a cache key without the token keys raises `ValueError` naming the file and the row, and a `null` trial count is never read as all the token trials (review iter-436 must-fix 1). `.save` writes a pair when its trials are above 0, in that order after the token keys, so a file it writes loads back as the same `Stats`. `calibrate_from_results`: a row may carry `cached_input_tokens` and `cache_write_tokens`, either or both, only beside its `input_tokens` and `output_tokens`, each that one trial's own count, an integer `>= 0` that is not a bool, so `null` raises rather than reading as no count
- v1.602 per-item outcomes (row GATE1b): `item_outcomes(rows: Iterable[dict], *, dataset_sha256: str) -> list[dict]` gives one outcome record per result row, in row order, so that two routes can be compared on the same items (4.7, row GATE1c). Each row is checked as `calibrate_from_results` checks it and must also carry `task`, `model` and `item`, each a non-empty `str`, as the outcome matrix requires (12.1) and as `paired_promotion` takes an item ID; `dataset_sha256` is a `str` of 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits, the sha256 of the labeled file's bytes; anything else raises `ValueError` before a record is returned, and no row is changed. A record is a dict with the keys `task`, `slice`, `route`, `item`, `correct` and `dataset_sha256`, in that order: the row's `task`, its `slice` or None when it has none (absent or null), its `model` (a model, variant, cascade or procedure ID), its `item`, its outcome by `calibrate_from_results`'s rule (`correct`, or `prediction == gold`) and the hash. A sliced row gives one record, not one per stats key. So the records hold exactly the trials the stats count: an item on which a route's call raised a provider error is a `False` outcome when its row says so and absent when the results file leaves it out, and calibrating adds no rule of its own (review iter-449 should-fix 3(c)). `calibrate_from_results`, `Stats`, its methods and its file format are v1.601's: the hash is kept in the records only, since a stats file merges the counts of every results file calibrated into it and one hash cannot name them. `model_routing.__all__` gains `item_outcomes`, after `PromotionCheck`
- v1.626 measured latency (row LAT1a): beside its counts, `Stats` keeps, per `(task, model_id)`, the time in milliseconds of each trial whose time was recorded, so that a later version can hold a route to a latency bar on the task (rows LAT1b and LAT1c). At v1.626 no rule of 5.2, 7 or 13 reads them, so every decision, record and result is v1.625's. `.add(task, model_id, successes, trials, *, ..., latencies_ms=None)`: `None`, no time, or a `list` or `tuple` of 1 to `trials` values, one per timed trial of this call, each a finite `int` or `float` `>= 0` that is not a `bool` and that a `float` can hold (checked as `cost_usd` is, v1.577), stored as a `float`; anything else, an empty sequence, a `str` and a time with 0 trials included, raises `ValueError` naming `latencies_ms`, and nothing is added when `add` raises. Any key may hold them, a cascade's and a procedure's included, since a trial's time is the whole route's, from the call to its answer, an escalation or a tool call in it included. A trial's time counts whether or not the trial succeeded, since a caller waits for a wrong answer as for a right one, while `report`'s percentiles (8.3) read `ok` attempts only, so the two can differ on the same calls
- v1.626 `.latencies(task, model_id) -> tuple[float, ...]` returns the key's times sorted ascending, `()` when none are recorded. `.p95_latency_ms(task, model_id) -> float | None` returns their 95th percentile by `report`'s nearest-rank rule (8.3): of the `n` sorted times, the one at index `max(0, ceil(0.95 * n) - 1)`, so it is a time one of the trials took, the slowest of them while `n` is below 20 and the second slowest at 20, and `None` when none is recorded, never 0. `.merge` joins the two sides' times; `.get`, `.items()`, `.tokens`, `.mean_tokens`, `.cache_tokens` and the other methods are v1.625's. A stated limit: a key holds one value per timed trial, so a stats file grows with them, and the percentile of a few trials is only that: at v1.626 no `min_samples` applies to it (from 5.2 v1.628 the latency bar reads it only once the key holds the call's `min_samples` times)
- v1.626 files and calibration: a `Stats.load` row may carry `latencies_ms`, a JSON array checked as `.add` checks it, so `null`, a number, a string, an empty array, more values than the row's `trials`, or a value that is a bool, negative or not a number raises `ValueError` naming the file and the row. `.save` writes it, sorted ascending, as the row's last key, after any cache keys, only for a key holding at least one time, so a `Stats` without one saves v1.625's bytes and a file it writes loads back as the same `Stats`. `calibrate_from_results`: a row may carry `latency_ms`, its one trial's time, a number checked as above, so `null` raises rather than reading as no time; it is checked with every row check, before the returned `Stats` exists, and a sliced row (v1.511) adds it under both keys. `item_outcomes` (v1.602) checks rows by `calibrate_from_results`, so it refuses the same rows, and its records gain no key. A results file without the key gives v1.625's stats bit for bit, and the `calibrate` command (10) needs no change: its printed table is unchanged, and the file it writes carries the times of the rows that had them. Where a trial's time comes from is the caller's to say: an attempt record's `latency_ms` (8.1) is one attempt's, and a call that falls back makes several, so a route's time is what the caller measured from its call to its answer (row LAT1c says so in the README); from 8.3 v1.637 (row LAT2) `audited_results` gives each row the time its route entry took to its answer

### 4.4 Priors (`priors.py`)
- Leaderboard numbers are not agreement rates, so priors NEVER clear a bar. They only order candidates when nothing has been measured (cold start) and tell you which models to calibrate first
- `Priors.load(path)` reads `{"categories": {name: {"metric": str, "source": str, "as_of": str, "scores": {model_id: number}}}}`; `Priors(categories: dict)` takes the same inner dict
- `.score(category, model_id) -> float | None`; unknown category or model returns `None`
- `.ranked(category) -> list[str]` model IDs by descending score, ties by ascending ID

### 4.5 Procedures (`procedures.py`, v1.576, row PROC1a)
- Why: a recurring job's fixed steps (submit, poll, batch, shape a result) can run as code instead of model turns, so that work costs no tokens; Uber's code-mode skills are the public case (`research/production-lessons.md`). A procedure is that code with a declared bound on its model calls and tool calls, routed later as one candidate route among the models (row PROC1b). It is a bounded callable, not an agent runtime, and this version adds the object and its run alone: no router, executor, record, report, evidence file or README transcript changes, and the README `## Layout` block gains the module's line, since it names every `model_routing/*.py` (review iter-423 must-fix 1)
- `@dataclass(frozen=True) class Procedure`: `Procedure(name, version, fn, *, max_model_calls, max_tool_calls, model=None)`, the last three keyword-only. `name` and `version` are each a `str` matching `[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*`, the variant-name pattern (4.1), so neither holds `@`, `+`, `/`, `:` or a space; `fn` is callable; `max_model_calls` and `max_tool_calls` are each an `int` that is not a `bool` and is `>= 0`; `model` is `None` or a non-empty `str` holding no `+` and no whitespace and not starting with `proc:`, the ID of the one registry route the procedure calls, for example `vendor/model` or `vendor/model@variant`: opaque here, as a registry ID is (4.1), and checked against the registry by row PROC1b, and never another procedure's ID, since a procedure calls a model route (review iter-423 should-fix 2). `model` is `None` exactly when `max_model_calls` is 0, so a procedure that calls a model names it and one that names a model may call it. Anything else raises `ValueError` at construction
- `.id` is the route ID: `proc:<name>@<version>` without a model, `proc:<name>@<version>+<model>` with one. A new version or another model is another ID, so stats keyed by it (row PROC1b) never carry an old version's or another model's counts, as a variant's never carry its base's (4.1 v1.572). The ID is the procedure's identity, its name, version and model: `fn` and the two bounds are not in it, so two procedures that differ only in them share an ID, and a change to the code or a bound comes with a new `version`, or PROC1b's stats would mix the two (review iter-423 should-fix 1). The row's `register_procedure(name, version, fn)` is this constructor: there is no module-level registry, so two routers in one process never share a registration
- `@dataclass(frozen=True) class ProcedureResult`: `output: str`, `tool_calls: int = 0`, `tool_cost_usd: float = 0.0`, what `fn` returns. `output` is a `str`; `tool_calls` an `int` that is not a `bool` and is `>= 0`; `tool_cost_usd` an `int` or `float` that is not a `bool`, is finite and is `>= 0`, stored as a `float`; anything else raises `ValueError` at construction. The procedure counts its own tool calls and their cost, since the tools are its own code: the library checks the declared bound on what it reports and cannot see the calls
- `@dataclass(frozen=True) class ProcedureRun`: `route: str` (the procedure's `.id`), `output: str`, `model_calls: int`, `tool_calls: int`, `tool_cost_usd: float`; `class ProcedureLimitError(Exception)`
- `Procedure.run(value, call) -> ProcedureRun` calls `fn(value, handle)` once, `value` passed as given. `call` takes the messages of one model call and returns its text; v1.578 (row PROC1c) makes it the executor's call of the named model (7 v1.578). `handle(messages)` raises `ProcedureLimitError` once the run has ended (after `fn` returns or raises, so a handle kept by `fn` is dead) or when the call would be number `max_model_calls + 1`, in either case before `call` is reached, and the ended run first, so a kept handle reports it even when its call would also be over the bound (review iter-423 should-fix 3); otherwise it counts the call and returns `call(messages)`, both passed unchanged, so a call that raises still counts. An exception that `fn` or `call` raises propagates unchanged. Then a return value that is not a `ProcedureResult` raises `ValueError`, and a `tool_calls` above `max_tool_calls` raises `ProcedureLimitError`, each naming the procedure's ID; else the run returns a `ProcedureRun` whose `route` is `.id`, with the output, the model calls counted and the result's tool calls and cost. Each run has its own handle and count, so one procedure runs any number of times; a handle is for one thread, since its count holds no lock, so `fn` makes its calls from the thread that runs it
- `model_routing.__all__` gains `Procedure`, `ProcedureResult`, `ProcedureRun` and `ProcedureLimitError`, after `evaluate_delegation`
- Test status: `tests/test_procedures.py` was committed before the module under a module-level `pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True, raises=ModuleNotFoundError)`, which the implementing commit removes
- Not in this version: the demo, the README paragraph and the note's line (row PROC1d; done in v1.580, 11). v1.577 (row PROC1b) routes a procedure as a candidate at its measured cost (5.2 v1.577) and keeps its counts and cost under its route ID (4.3 v1.577), and v1.578 (row PROC1c) runs one in the executor with its fallback (7 v1.578) and records its keys `procedure`, `procedure_version`, `model_calls`, `tool_calls` and `tool_cost_usd` (8.1 v1.578)

### 4.6 Budgets (`budget.py`, v1.595, row B1a)
- Why: an alert does not stop spend, and a team that runs the library in production needs a limit it enforces itself; Uber's spend tiers and Grab's per-key gateway limits are the public cases (`research/production-lessons.md`). This version keeps each budget's spend inside one process; a limit shared by many processes still needs a gateway or the provider's own.
- `@dataclass(frozen=True) class Budget`: `Budget(name, limit_usd, mode, window="total", task=None, tags={}, strict=False)`, `strict` from v1.597 (row B1c). `name` a non-empty `str`; `limit_usd` an `int` or `float` that is not a `bool`, finite as a `float` and above 0, stored as a `float`; `mode` `"warn"`, `"refuse"` or, from v1.596, `"downgrade"`; `window` `"total"`, the ledger's whole life, or, from v1.596, `"day"` or `"month"`, a UTC calendar day or month (row B1b); `task` None or a non-empty `str`; `tags` a mapping of `str` to `str`, stored as a new `dict`. Anything else raises `ValueError` at construction.
- `Budget.applies(task, tags) -> bool`: True when `task` is None or the call's task and the call's tags hold every pair of `tags`. So a budget with neither takes every call, one on `{"tool": "a"}` only the calls tagged so, and a run's calls share one when the caller tags each with the run's root ID, a delegated call keeping the caller's tags (7 v1.11).
- `load_budgets(path) -> tuple[Budget, ...]` reads `{"budgets": [ {field: value, ...}, ... ]}` with the six fields above and, from v1.597, `strict`, `name`, `limit_usd` and `mode` required, a JSON `null` task read as None; a file that is not that object, a row that is not an object, a missing or unknown key or a repeated name raises `ValueError`.
- `class BudgetLedger(budgets=())`: a list or tuple of `Budget` with unique names, else `ValueError`. Under one `threading.Lock` it keeps each budget's settled spend and the holds of the calls in flight. `.budgets` is the tuple; `.spent_usd(name)` the settled spend and `.held_usd(name)` the `math.fsum` of the live holds' amounts (each its estimate, or from v1.597 its bound on a strict budget, review iter-445 nit 2), each a `float`, `ValueError` for a name it lacks; `.events` a tuple of new dicts, the warn crossings in order.
  - `.reserve(task, tags, estimate_usd, model=None, at=None)`: for each `refuse` budget that applies, in the ledger's order, then (v1.596) each `downgrade` budget that applies, in the ledger's order, when its spend plus its holds plus `estimate_usd`, each of the window that holds `at`, is over its limit, it raises `BudgetExceeded` for the first such budget and holds nothing; else it holds `estimate_usd` on every budget that applies, of any mode, each in its window, and returns an opaque hold. So a `refuse` budget that would be passed always refuses, whatever a `downgrade` budget says.
  - `.settle(hold, cost_usd)` releases the hold and adds `cost_usd` to the spend of each budget it was held on, in the window it was held in; a hold settled again raises `ValueError`. `.charge(task, tags, cost_usd, at=None)` adds a cost spent without a hold to each budget that applies, in the window that holds `at`, and never refuses. Each amount of the three is an `int` or `float` that is not a `bool`, finite and `>= 0`, else `ValueError`.
  - Warn crossings: when an add first takes a `warn` budget's spend to at least 0.5, 0.8 or 1.0 times its limit, the ledger appends `{"budget": name, "share": s, "spent_usd": spend, "limit_usd": limit}` for each share it crosses, in share order, so each share fires once per window and one add can fire several: once in the ledger's life for a `total` budget, and once in each UTC day or month for a `day` or `month` budget, whose event gains a last key, `window`, the window's label (v1.596). A `refuse` or `downgrade` budget writes none.
  - v1.596 windows (row B1b): `at` is None or a `str` that `datetime.fromisoformat` reads once a trailing `Z` is replaced by `+00:00`, else `ValueError`, checked whenever it is not None; a timestamp with no offset is read as UTC, and one with an offset is converted to UTC. A `day` budget's window is the UTC date of `at`, labelled `YYYY-MM-DD`, and a `month` budget's its UTC year and month, `YYYY-MM`; `at` None reads the current UTC time, and a `total` budget has its one window whatever `at` is. `.spent_usd(name, at=None)` and `.held_usd(name, at=None)` give the spend and the live holds of the window that holds `at`. A hold keeps the window it was reserved in, so a call that starts before midnight UTC and settles after it is spent in the day it started, and a hold of one window never counts against another. A past window's spend stays in the ledger, one number per budget and window, and so do a `warn` budget's fired shares and events, at most three of each per window; nothing expires (review iter-444 should-fix 1). `datetime.fromisoformat` reads more forms from Python 3.11 than on 3.10 (a basic or a week date, for example), so such a form is read or refused as the running Python does; the executor's default `now`, `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.fffZ`, and the extended forms with or without an offset read alike on 3.10 to 3.14 (review iter-444 nit 1).
  - v1.597 strict (row B1c): `strict` is a `bool`, `False` unless set, and `True` only with mode `refuse` or `downgrade`, since a `warn` budget refuses nothing; anything else raises `ValueError`. `billing_bound(model) -> float | None` is the most one call of `model` can cost by `Model.cost` when its billing is bounded: its `provider_options` hold at least one of `max_tokens`, `max_completion_tokens` and `max_output_tokens`, each an `int` >= 1 that is not a `bool`, the largest of them, `m`, capping the output, and the input is at most `max(context_window - m, 0)` tokens, since a provider refuses a request whose input and output maximum pass the context window. The bound is the largest `Model.cost` at output `m` over that input and each price tier threshold under it, each input all uncached, all cached reads or all cache writes, so a lower tier or cache price never lowers it; a model whose options hold none of the three keys, or one of them with any other value, has None, no bound. `.reserve(..., bound_usd=None)`: a strict budget that applies checks and holds `bound_usd` where any other checks and holds `estimate_usd`, and refuses a `bound_usd` of None, raising `BudgetExceeded` with `.unbounded` True; `bound_usd` is None or an amount like the others. `.settle_unpriced(hold)` releases the hold of a call whose cost is not known: a strict budget adds the bound it held and any other 0.0, as v1.595 settled such a call, each in the hold's window, and a hold settled again raises `ValueError` (review iter-443 nit 2); `.settle` still refuses a cost of None. So a strict budget's spend passes its limit only when a provider bills past the bound (more output than `m`, or input past the window) or the ledger is charged past it (`.charge`). With no strict budget every check, hold, settle and event is v1.596's.
